newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Dunblane remembers murdered children one year on.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dunblane remembers murdered children one year on.

text.p: The release of a black-and-white photo showing the gap-toothed smiles of Gwen Mayor's Primary One class brought home the full scale of the horror.
Until then the slaughter of 16 five- and six-year-olds and their teacher by a deranged gunman was almost too terrible to comprehend. Until then, the innocent victims were abstract.
The photograph made them real. One year later, the photograph still brings tears to the eyes but the town of Dunblane is recovering.
The school itself looks as unremarkable as it was before March 13, 1996, when ex-scoutmaster Thomas Hamilton burst in on Primary One's gym class and opened up with four handguns.

It is at first hard to pick out the school's driveway from the prosperous, middle-class houses that surround it. The pavements outside are no longer carpeted with bouquets sent from a world shocked by news of the massacre.
A small sign has been posted at the school boundaries -- even today there is no real gate or fence -- asking that flowers be delivered to the cemetery.

Boys play football in the green fields that back onto the grounds. The gymnasium where Hamilton wreaked his vengeance on the community that had rejected him has been torn down and trees planted in its place.
REMEMBERING THE DEAD

The school and the families of the victims have asked to be left in peace on the anniversary. School will open an hour late on March 13 to give the children and families time to visit the site of the gym.
In the evening, residents of the town will place a single candle in their front windows.

The parents of the slain children are marking the date in various ways. Some have never spoken publicly of their grief and remain withdrawn. Others fought for a nationwide ban on handguns, which the government, controversially, pushed through.

A few have chosen to talk about their battle to recover. Several helped make a film about their lives and memories of their children, which will be broadcast in Britain on March 12. Others collaborated on a book.
"Most families are trying to make it as normal a day as possible," Karen Scott, who lost her daughter Hannah, told a rare news conference held to launch the film.
"The pain does not and probably will not go away," her husband David added. "We as a family will go to the cathedral. We may go to the cemetery."
Most of the families meet regularly, on Thursday nights, to discuss their grief and to try to start enjoying life once again.
"Only recently we've started talking to each other about what happened precisely that day," Karen Scott says in the film, produced for Britain's Meridian Broadcasting.
"For a long time we couldn't contemplate discussing it. It just wasn't possible."
But Scott said sharing what happened to them that day, when some of the parents were kept hours waiting to hear what had happened to their children, had created a bond.

Les Morton, whose daughter Emily was killed, said he had found a new friendship in Mick North, who lost Sophie. Both single men -- North was recently widowed -- they have clearly found comfort in one another's company.

"He's such a lovely guy and I think to myself that nine months ago he would have been a lovely guy as well and yet I never even took the time," Morton says. "It's just tremendously sad that it's taken this tragedy to bring these things out."
In the film the group are shown laughing and having a drink in one of the local pubs.

"Some people removed from the situation find it a little strange, you know -- what are they doing laughing...they should be home dressed in black'," said Duncan McLennan, whose daughter Abigail was killed.
But Kareen Turner said being able to laugh again was the point. "If we were all to sit there and be sad and to cry, then the group wouldn't be there."
MIXED EMOTIONS
But there are moments of guilt for all.
Some children at the school asked if it was all right to celebrate Christmas last year. One boy agonised over whether he should have a birthday party a few days before the anniversary.
Alison and Ian Irvine, who lost their son Ross, learned a few months ago that they were expecting twins.
"I'm full of conflicting emotions," she told the Times newspaper. "I feel disloyal having another child. It can't compensate. Ross is dead.

"But then again, I think if I didn't have them I would be disloyal as well to his memory...If Ross had been here he would have been over the moon at having two girls -- I'm sure they're going to be girls."
Surviving siblings sometimes still had troubling dealing with the loss, too. McLennan said his daughters Rachel and Lauren now shared a single bed every night.
"Lauren has a lot of anger still. And Rachel is just terrified that something will happen either to Liz or myself or Lauren. She won't go anywhere in the house on their own."
Liz McLennan said the families had learned to really value their children. "We have to make the most of every second we have with them."
"Put it this way," interrupted Duncan. "If it's a choice between doing the garden or playing with the kids, then playing with the kids has to come first."
Barbara Dunn said she had fought the temptation to become more protective of her three-year-old son. "We can't cocoon him," she said.
"I think it would be very easy to say 'yes, you're not going anywhere'," she added. "He'll be starting school soon. I'm dreading the day."
